extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. This is achieved by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.citeAs: Lin, T.Y., Maire, M., Belongie, S., Hays, J., Perona, P., Ramanan, D., Dollár, P. and Zitnick, C.L., 2014. Microsoft coco: Common objects in context. In European conference on computer vision (pp. 740-755). Springer, Cham.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created by harvesting a large set of images containing contextual relationships and non-iconic object views. Images were collected from Flickr using scene-based queries and pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') to find non-iconic images. Additionally, images were retrieved via Google or Bing image search. The collection involved filtering out iconic images to ensure a majority of non-iconic images.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Photos from Flickr, Google Image Search, and Bing Image Search.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed across dataset splits. Images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize duplicates. For images with more than 10-15 instances of a category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment, which were ignored during evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were filtered to remove iconic images. Near-duplicate images were removed. The dataset was split into training, validation, and testing sets. A subset of 80 categories was used for the 2014 release, excluding 11 categories due to difficulty or ambiguity in labeling.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation was performed using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) in three stages: 1) Category Labeling: Workers indicated presence of object categories using a hierarchical approach (8 workers per image). 2) Instance Spotting: Workers placed crosses on instances of labeled categories (8 workers per image). 3) Instance Segmentation: Workers segmented individual object instances. A training task was required for workers. A verification step was added where 3-5 workers judged segmentation quality; poor segmentations were discarded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker quality was analyzed by comparing crowd workers to expert workers. The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any expert worker. Precision and recall were measured. A leave-one-out evaluation procedure was used to assess precision. Workers who completed the most jobs had the highest precision. Segmentations were verified by multiple workers, with a threshold of 4 out of 5 favorable votes required for acceptance.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple (8 workers for category labeling and instance spotting; 1 worker for segmentation, verified by 3-5 workers)
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Specific demographics not provided.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into two releases. The first half was released in 2014, and the second half was scheduled for release in 2015. The dataset is expected to evolve and grow over time, with up-to-date information available online.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance scene understanding and object recognition, which are critical for computer vision applications. It addresses challenges like non-iconic views and contextual reasoning, which reflect real-world complexity.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses on 'thing' categories and excludes 'stuff' categories (materials, objects with no clear boundaries) to enable precise localization. This may introduce bias against scenes dominated by 'stuff'. The selection of categories was influenced by votes from co-authors and children, potentially reflecting specific cultural or linguistic biases in category definitions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The 2014 release is limited to 80 categories, excluding 11 due to difficulty or ambiguity. The dataset contains 'crowds' where individual instances are not segmented, which are ignored in evaluation. The dataset may contain noise from crowd workers, although verification steps were taken. Models trained on this data may not always perform better on easier datasets due to the difficulty of non-iconic images.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning for object detection, instance segmentation, and scene understanding tasks.
